449.title: Ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent (2.4–2.5)
449.hook: Patanjali defines the root of every affliction as four simple mix-ups, and the first is mistaking the passing for the permanent
449.howItsDone: In yoga and Vedanta teaching, avidya is treated as the root problem, and students practice discernment, noticing what passes and what remains, as the way to loosen it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the kleshas, five roots, avidya first, then I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging. Today, the root under all the roots.

You buy a new phone and, for a week, it feels like it will make you happy forever. You get a compliment and replay it for days, as if it settled who you are. You lose an argument and feel, all afternoon, like that's the permanent truth about you. None of these were lies, exactly. They were mix-ups: something passing treated as something lasting. Patanjali puts that kind of mix-up at the very bottom of human trouble.
screen: `A NEW PHONE: HAPPY FOREVER.` → `A COMPLIMENT: WHO I AM.` → `THE PASSING, TAKEN AS LASTING.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.4: ignorance is the field for the others, whether they are dormant, thin, interrupted or fully active. Field, kshetra, like soil: I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging all grow out of it, in four states. Dormant, asleep like seeds in winter. Thin, weakened by practice. Interrupted, pushed down for a while by a stronger feeling. Or active, in full bloom. Then sutra 2.5 defines avidya with four mix-ups. Taking the impermanent as permanent. The impure as pure. What brings pain as pleasant. And what is not the self as the self. Avidya isn't an empty space where knowledge should be. Vidya means knowledge; a-vidya is its opposite, an active wrong knowing that feels completely true from the inside. The commentator Vyasa compares it to an enemy, who isn't merely the absence of a friend but the opposite of one. The last mix-up is the deepest: taking the body, the mind, the moods, the roles as the self, when in Patanjali's system the self is the seer, the one who watches them. You've already practiced the remedy, in chapter one: the seer resting in itself. This is the same truth from the other side. The trouble begins the moment the seer seems to become what it sees.
screen: `THE FIELD THE OTHERS GROW IN.` · `DORMANT, THIN, INTERRUPTED, ACTIVE.` · `FOUR MIX-UPS.` · then, large: `NOT-SELF TAKEN AS SELF.`

segments.voice: Notice something in you that feels permanent right now, a mood, a worry, a sense of who you are today, and ask lightly: has this always been here, and will it always be? Watch it for a few breaths and see whether it shifts, even a little. Then notice what has been watching it the whole time, and rest there.
Ignorance. Avidya: not a lack of facts but a wrong knowing, taking the passing for the permanent, the painful for the pleasant, the not-self for the self.
Your line: avidya. The passing, mistaken for what lasts, and the not-self for the self. Day four hundred forty-nine, done.

450.title: I-ness (2.6)
450.hook: the second affliction hides in one tiny Sanskrit word, iva, 'as if'
450.howItsDone: In classical yoga, asmita is loosened through discernment between the seer and the seen, and teachers often have students notice the difference between awareness and the thoughts and roles it is aware of.

segments.voice: Yesterday: avidya, the passing taken for the permanent and the not-self taken for the self. Today, what grows first from that soil.

Put on a pair of rose-tinted glasses and, after a few minutes, you stop noticing them. The world just looks rosy. Ask what color the sky is, and you'll say pink, and mean it. You're not lying. You've simply forgotten there's anything between your eyes and the sky. The glasses become part of how you see, and then, without your noticing, part of who you think you are. Sutra 2.6 is about that forgetting.
screen: `ROSE-TINTED GLASSES.` → `THE SKY IS PINK.` → `YOU FORGET THE GLASSES.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.6: drig darshana shaktyor ekatmata iva asmita. I-ness is when the seer and the instrument of seeing seem to be one self. Drig, the seer: pure awareness, the purusha you met on day four hundred thirty-one. Darshana shakti, the power of seeing, here meaning the instrument, the mind, through which the seer sees. Ekatmata, one-self-ness. Then the small, crucial word: iva, as if. They are not one. They only seem to be. Asmita comes from asmi, I am. It's the felt sense of me: this body, these thoughts, these moods, my story, bundled together and taken to be the one who sees. The glasses and the eyes, fused. Notice the order. First the mistake, ignorance. Then, from it, the mistaken me, the one who will want things tomorrow and fear things the day after. Asmita isn't arrogance. A shy person has just as much of it as a loud one. It's the basic glue that sticks awareness to the mind's contents. You met the word in chapter one, in the subtlest stage of samadhi with seed: the bare sense of I am. There it was the finest object of absorption. Here it's shown as a knot. Commentators hold the two together: the sense of I am is subtle, and it still isn't the seer.
screen: `DRIG: THE SEER. DARSHANA: THE INSTRUMENT.` · `IVA: AS IF.` · `NOT ARROGANCE: THE GLUE.` · then, large: `THE GLASSES TAKEN FOR THE EYES.`

segments.voice: Say silently, I am, and notice what comes with it: a feeling in the chest, a picture of your face, a name, a role. Then notice that you are aware of all of it, and gently ask whether the one who sees is one more thing on the list. You don't need an answer; let the question loosen the glue a little.
I-ness. Asmita, sutra 2.6: the seer and the mind it sees through seem to be one self. Seem, as if, iva, is the key.
Your line: asmita. The glasses, taken for the eyes, until you remember they're there. See you tomorrow.

451.title: Attraction and aversion (2.7–2.8)
451.hook: two sutras, almost mirror images, explain why the mind keeps chasing and keeps running
451.tomorrow: fear of death — even in the wise
451.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages ask students to watch raga and dvesha in daily life, pausing before acting on a like or dislike, and the Bhagavad Gita also names them as obstacles on the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: asmita, I-ness, the seer and the mind as if fused, like glasses forgotten on your face. Today, what that I starts doing.

You walk past a bakery and smell cinnamon rolls, and before you've decided anything, you've slowed down. Your feet know. Somewhere in your memory is a cinnamon roll that was very, very good. Then a dentist's drill starts up down the hall, and your shoulders rise. Somewhere in your memory is a bad afternoon in a chair. Nobody chose either reaction. They were waiting. Patanjali says exactly where.
screen: `CINNAMON ROLLS: YOU SLOW DOWN.` → `A DENTIST'S DRILL: YOU TENSE.` → `NEITHER WAS CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.7: sukha anushayi ragah. Attraction follows pleasure. Sutra 2.8: duhkha anushayi dveshah. Aversion follows pain. Two short sutras, almost mirror images. The key word is anushayi: following after, or resting upon. Attraction rests on the memory of pleasure. Aversion rests on the memory of pain. The commentator Vyasa puts it plainly: raga is the thirst for pleasure in one who remembers pleasure, and dvesha is the resentment toward pain in one who remembers pain. So these aren't random moods. They're grooves left by experience, pulling and pushing the mind in advance. And who got the pleasure, who got hurt? The I, yesterday's asmita. Without a me to have pleasures and pains, attraction and aversion would have nothing to hold on to. That's one reading of why they come third and fourth on the list. In these two sutras, Patanjali doesn't call pleasure itself the affliction. A cinnamon roll is a cinnamon roll. The affliction is the grip: a memory deciding for you before you've looked at what's actually in front of you. Attraction narrows the world to what you want. Aversion narrows it to what you're avoiding. Either way, you see less. And the two are partners. A strong like often has a matching dislike close behind it: wanting the praise, dreading the criticism. Practice doesn't erase them in a day. It thins them, as sutra 2.2 promised, one noticed grip at a time.
screen: `RAGA FOLLOWS PLEASURE.` · `DVESHA FOLLOWS PAIN.` · `GROOVES LEFT BY MEMORY.` · then, large: `THE GRIP, NOT THE ROLL.`

segments.voice: Watch for tiny pulls and pushes as you sit: an itch you want to scratch, a thought of something nice later, a sound you wish would stop. Name each one gently, raga or dvesha, and wait one breath before doing anything. Often the pull fades by itself; if not, act slowly, knowing what moved you.
Anushayi, following after, resting upon. Raga, attraction, follows the memory of pleasure; dvesha, aversion, follows the memory of pain: grooves that pull and push the mind.
Your line: raga, dvesha. The pull and the push, both resting on memory. That's day four hundred fifty-one.

452.title: Fear of death — even in the wise (2.9)
452.hook: the fifth affliction runs by its own momentum, and Patanjali says it's there even in the wise
452.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often study the five afflictions with a teacher, one sutra at a time, alongside the classical commentary. Some Hindus also keep practices that face death directly, such as remembering God's name daily and hearing scripture read at the end of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: anushayi. Raga and dvesha, the pull toward what was sweet and the push from what hurt, both resting on memory. Today, the last of the five afflictions.
screen: `RAGA, DVESHA — THE PULL AND THE PUSH.`

segments.voice: An elevator drops half a floor and catches itself. Everyone inside grabs the rail. The nervous intern grabs it. So does the surgeon who has stood beside a hundred deathbeds and talks about dying calmly at dinner parties. Nobody decided to grab. The hands just went. That grab is older than any opinion about death. Four of the five afflictions have had their day. Today the fifth, with a phrase that should surprise anyone who thinks study is a cure.
screen: `THE ELEVATOR DROPS.` → `EVERY HAND GRABS THE RAIL.` → `THE FIFTH AFFLICTION.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.9 calls it abhinivesha. The word carries a sense of settling into, digging in: clinging to life, the wish to go on. Patanjali gives it two descriptions. First, svarasa-vahi: it flows by its own momentum, the way a river runs downhill without anyone pushing. Second, and this is the startling part, it is established even in the wise. Vidushah api. Even in the one who knows. The classical commentary, traditionally credited to Vyasa, fills it in with a line every creature seems to carry: may I not stop being, may I go on. Then it points at something tiny. A worm that has only just hatched already shrinks from danger. It has never died in this life. So where did it learn the fear? The commentator's answer is memory: the trace of deaths before, carried forward from earlier lives. Some modern readers hear instinct there instead. Either way, the fear is there before any learning. Patanjali doesn't call the fear shameful. He doesn't say smart people get over it. He puts it in the wise and leaves it there, a plain reminder that reading alone doesn't dissolve it. The next two sutras say what works on the afflictions: tracing them back to where they start, and meditation. Day to day, abhinivesha is rarely about dying. It's the grip on a job you've outgrown, an old argument, the last scroll before sleep. Small endings, and the same grab at the rail.
screen: `ABHINIVESHA — DIGGING IN.` · `IT FLOWS BY ITS OWN MOMENTUM.` · `EVEN IN THE WISE.` · `THE NEWBORN WORM ALREADY FLINCHES.` · then, large: `THE SAME GRAB, IN SMALL ENDINGS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath run on its own, and after a few rounds notice the little pause at the bottom of the out-breath, and whether something in you hurries to grab the next breath. No need to hold or stretch the pause; just let each out-breath finish and watch the next one come by itself. If anything feels uncomfortable, breathe normally.
Svarasa-vahi, flowing by its own momentum, like a river downhill. Abhinivesha, the clinging to going on, runs by itself this way, and stays even in the wise.
Your line: abhinivesha. Even the wise feel the grab, and there's no shame in it. Go gently; see you tomorrow.

453.title: Karma and its fruit (2.12–2.14)
453.hook: action leaves a deposit, rooted in the afflictions, and it ripens as a birth, a life span and what you live through
453.howItsDone: In Hindu teaching, karma is action whose results ripen over time, in this life or a later one, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present practice as the way to weaken the afflictions that make stored action sprout.

segments.voice: Yesterday: svarasa-vahi. Abhinivesha, the clinging to life that runs by itself, even in the wise. Today, what the afflictions do over time.

Somewhere in a kitchen drawer is a paper packet of seeds. Tomato, maybe, bought three springs ago and forgotten. Dry, light, a little dusty. Nothing seems to be happening in there. And yet tip those seeds into wet soil next week, and a good number will wake up and become exactly what they were always going to be. Not a rose. Tomatoes. Patanjali has named the five afflictions. Now he asks what they do over time, and his answer sounds a lot like that drawer.
screen: `A FORGOTTEN PACKET OF SEEDS.` → `NOTHING SEEMS TO HAPPEN.` → `WET SOIL, AND THEY WAKE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.12 gives the drawer a name: karmashaya. Karma is action. Ashaya is a resting place, a container. The storehouse of action. Every deed leaves something behind, and the storehouse holds it. Its root, Patanjali says, is the afflictions, and it will be lived out either in this birth, the one that's seen, or in one unseen. Sutra 2.13 says how it ripens. As long as the root is there, stored action comes to fruit in three ways: the kind of birth, how long that life lasts, and what is experienced in it. And 2.14 gives the flavor of that fruit: joy, if the action was meritorious; pain, if it wasn't. Notice the picture underneath. There's no judge in the sutras' account, no scorekeeper adding up points. It's closer to farming: seeds, soil, time, harvest. The classical commentary adds a homely image. Rice still in its husk can sprout, but once the husk is stripped away, or the seed is roasted, it won't come up. The afflictions are the husk. Take away not seeing clearly, take away I-ness and grasping, and the seeds in the storehouse lose the power to grow. So this isn't fatalism. It's an argument for practice. And the storehouse fills quietly: the sharp reply, the patient one, the favor nobody saw, each a small deposit.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you did yesterday, kind or unkind, and notice what it left in you: a warmth, a tightness, a replay. That's the deposit; just see it clearly, the way you'd hold a seed in your palm, without judging or fixing it. Then set it down and come back to the breath, which is happening now, not yesterday.
Karmashaya, the storehouse of action. Every deed leaves a deposit there, rooted in the afflictions, and it ripens as a birth, a life span and an experience.
Your line: the storehouse. Every deed a seed, and practice works on the husk. Day four hundred fifty-three, done.

454.title: "To the discerning, all is suffering" (2.15–2.17)
454.hook: the gloomiest-sounding line in the sutras turns out to be about sensitivity, and about the pain that hasn't come yet
454.tomorrow: The purpose of the world: experience and liberation
454.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often present 2.15–2.17 as a medical outline, the illness and its cause, followed later by the cure and the remedy, and students reflect on it in study and in meditation on the difference between awareness and what it is aware of.

segments.voice: Yesterday: karmashaya, the storehouse. Action leaves a seed, and the afflictions are the husk that lets it sprout. Today, a line that sounds gloomy at first.

An eyelash falls onto your cheek. You don't notice it all afternoon. The same eyelash lands in your eye, and suddenly you can't read, can't talk, can't think of anything else. Same eyelash. Different place. Read fast, today's sutra sounds like Patanjali hated life. But the old commentary explains it with a picture very like this one, the eye and a tiny thread, and once you see it, the line stops sounding like despair. It starts sounding like a diagnosis.
screen: `AN EYELASH ON YOUR CHEEK.` → `THE SAME EYELASH IN YOUR EYE.` → `NOT DESPAIR. A DIAGNOSIS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.15 says: to the discerning, all is suffering. Duhkha. The one who sees clearly, the vivekin, finds pain even in pleasure, and Patanjali gives four reasons. Change: the sweet thing is already ending. Anxiety: while you have it, you fear losing it. Impressions: it leaves a groove that wants more. And the three qualities of nature, always pulling against each other, so nothing stays settled. The commentary, traditionally credited to Vyasa, explains who the discerning person is. Most people, it says, are like the rest of the body: a thread of wool lands on an arm or a leg and nothing is felt. The discerning person is like the eyeball. The same thread, and it hurts. So the line isn't a mood. It's about becoming sensitive enough to feel what was always there. Then the turn. Sutra 2.16 is three words in Sanskrit: heyam duhkham anagatam. The suffering not yet come is to be avoided. The past is done. The present is already being lived. Only the future is still open, and that is where practice works. And 2.17 names the cause: the joining of the seer and the seen. The pure awareness that watches, and everything it watches, mind included, tangled until awareness mistakes itself for what it sees. The commentary notices that this follows the order of medicine: the disease, its cause, the cure, the remedy. Today, the first two.

segments.voice: Notice one sensation, the weight of your hands, a sound in the room, an itch: that's the seen. Then notice that something is noticing it, and feel the difference between the sound and the hearing of it. When a thought comes, let it join the seen, one more thing in the room, and rest as the one watching.
Duhkha, suffering, pain, unease, the opposite of ease. Not a mood but a sensitivity, like the eye that feels the thread, and a turn toward the pain that hasn't come yet.
Your line: the seen and the seer. The disease and its cause have names now; the cure is coming. Until tomorrow.

455.title: The purpose of the world: experience and liberation (2.18–2.22)
455.hook: the seen world exists for the seer, for two things, experience and freedom, and it doesn't vanish when one person is done
455.howItsDone: In the Samkhya and Yoga schools, the world of nature is understood to exist for the sake of awareness, offering both experience and the chance of liberation; students study these sutras with the classical commentary and reflect on them in meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: duhkha, and your line, the seen and the seer. To the discerning, all is suffering, and the cause is the two tangled together. Today ends the week.

There's an old picture in the Samkhya Karika, a related text whose map of seer and seen the Yoga Sutras share. A dancer performs on a stage. She dances and dances, until the one watching has truly seen her. Then she stops, because the dance has done its work. Patanjali has named the cause of suffering: the seer and the seen, joined. You might expect him to call the seen the enemy, the trap to escape. He does something stranger. He asks what the whole show is for, and gives it a purpose.
screen: `A DANCER ON A STAGE.` → `SHE STOPS WHEN SHE'S TRULY SEEN.` → `WHAT IS THE SHOW FOR?`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.18 describes the seen: everything that can be watched, the mountains, the body, the senses, the mind itself. Its nature is light, activity and stillness, the three qualities of nature. And its purpose is two things: experience and liberation. Bhoga and apavarga. The world is there so the seer can taste it, and so the seer can finally be free of the confusion. Both, not one instead of the other. Then 2.20 describes the seer: pure seeing, nothing more. Though pure, it looks out through the ideas of the mind, and so it seems to take their color. And 2.21 is the short, bold line: the seen exists only for the seer's sake. Then 2.22 adds something tender. When one person's purpose is done, the world doesn't disappear. It stays, because it is shared with everyone else still dancing and watching. Nobody's freedom switches the lights off for the rest. Now the week, from the top. Ignorance: mistaking the passing for the permanent. I-ness: mistaking the instrument for the one who sees. Attraction and aversion, the pull and the push. Fear of death, even in the wise. Karma, the storehouse, where it all ripens. To the discerning, all is suffering. And today, the turn: the same world that tangles is there for freedom. Seven days of diagnosis, and the last one ends with a reason.
screen: `BHOGA AND APAVARGA.` · `THE SEER: PURE SEEING.` · `THE SEEN EXISTS FOR THE SEER.` · `IT STAYS FOR EVERYONE ELSE.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `FOR THE SEER.`

segments.voice: First, experience: let one sense fill up, the sounds in the room or the light through your eyelids, and taste it fully without grabbing. Then freedom: notice that the sound comes and goes, and the hearing stays. Move between the two, tasting and watching, as many times as you like.
Apavarga, release, liberation. In the Yoga Sutras, the seen exists for the seer, for two things: experience and liberation.
Your line: for the seer. Experience and liberation, both. That's the week, day four hundred fifty-five.
